amendments.rule: Reordered or discontinuous target tokens may occupy one unit when they realize one source item. Do not absorb unrelated intervening words into that unit. **Where English repeats one source function word because its scope is distributed across coordinated or emphatically repeated phrases or clauses, every English occurrence belongs to that source morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit.** `מִן` in `מִבּוֹא בְדָמִים וְהוֹשֵׁוַע` → *from bloodguiltiness, and from avenging* takes both occurrences of *from*, while the waw takes only *and*; `בִּי אֲנִי` → *upon me ... upon me* gives both occurrences of *upon* to the single preposition while the suffix and explicit pronoun take their respective *me*. The repeated English word is neither `added` nor reassigned to a neighboring source item merely to make the units contiguous. **And the repeated word need not be one the source writes.** Where another rule assigns a supplied English function word to a morpheme's unit — a preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own object under rule 44, or a word the ASV supplies for a bare nominal under rule 33 — and the ASV writes that same word again over an elliptical or gapped parallel member, the second occurrence belongs to that same morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit on exactly the terms above, however much stands between. `תְּבַקְשֶׁנָּה כַכָּסֶף וְכַמַּטְמוֹנִים תַּחְפְּשֶׂנָּה` → *search* ***for*** *her as* ***for*** *hid treasures* gives both *for*s to the verb, since the second stands for the searching the comparative clause elides, while each comparative `כְּ` takes only the *as* written for it. Do not read such a repetition as a second English word for the preposition, the conjunction or the comparative particle it stands beside, which would give one morpheme a two-word rendering the ASV writes for it nowhere else; and do not mark it `added` under rule 30, since the morpheme that licensed the first occurrence licenses this one. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the repeated word and ask whether what has gone is the reach of a rendering already placed in the clause, or a relation no morpheme there carries. **An explicit personal pronoun is read the same way where the ASV resumes it in a later clause of the same verse.** Where a following verbless clause writes no subject of its own and the ASV supplies the subject pronoun that an explicit `הוּא`, `הֵמָּה`, `אֲנִי` or the like standing earlier in the verse denotes, both occurrences belong to that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, exactly as rule 18 gives both pronouns of a twice-rendered suffix to the suffix and rule 20 gives both halves of an identifying formula to its one `הוּא`: `הֵמָּה סֹחֲרֵי יָדֵךְ ... בָּם סֹחֲרָיִךְ` → *they were the merchants of thy hand ... in these were* ***they*** *thy merchants* gives both *they*s to the one `הֵמָּה`, headed on the first. Such a pronoun is not `added`, and it does not join the predicate's unit: rule 20 hands the predicate the construction's copula and, in a presentative clause, its dummy *there*, and a referential pronoun is neither, so the clause's supplied *were* goes to the predicate while the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it. This governs a clause with no subject of its own: where a finite verb stands in the resumed clause it takes the English subject pronoun under rule 17, which is a pronoun realizing that verb's own person and number. **And where the Hebrew stands the pronoun is not part of the condition.** Hebrew postposes an explicit subject pronoun after its predicate and that predicate's adjuncts, often before a coordinated second subject, while English writes a subject before its verb; where the ASV writes the pronoun in both places it has realized one written morpheme twice, and both occurrences are that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, headed on the first English occurrence: `וְהִנֵּה נִצָּב עַל־עֹלָתוֹ הוּא וְכָל־שָׂרֵי מוֹאָב` → *and lo* ***he*** *was standing by his burnt offering,* ***he*** *and all the princes of Moab* gives both *he*s to the one `הוּא`, while `נִצָּב` keeps the *was standing* rule 20 leaves it and the coordinated subject keeps its own English. So read whether one written pronoun is realized twice rather than which side of the resumption it stands on, and do not hand the first occurrence to the predicate to make the units contiguous: rule 17's permission reaches a pronoun realizing a finite verb's own person and number, and a participle or other predicate morpheme in a verbless clause takes only the copula. **And the morpheme that denotes the resumed subject need not be a pronoun.** Where a common noun or a proper name written in the verse is the referent the ASV resumes, every English realization of that referent belongs to the noun's one possibly discontinuous unit on exactly the terms above, headed on the first English occurrence: `עַל־אֱלוֹהַּ נוֹרָא הוֹד` → ***God*** *hath upon* ***him*** *terrible majesty* gives both *God* and *him* to the one `אֱלוֹהַּ`, and `שַׁדַּי לֹא־מְצָאנֻהוּ שַׂגִּיא־כֹּחַ` → *Touching* ***the Almighty****, we cannot find him out;* ***He*** *is excellent in power* gives the resuming *He* to `שַׁדַּי`, while `שַׂגִּיא` keeps the *is excellent* rule 20 leaves it. This is the preceding paragraphs' own reasoning read for the morpheme that is actually written — the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it — since what licenses the English word is that the verse writes the referent, and not the part of speech the ASV first realized it by. Rule 17's ruling that a supplied lexical subject noun is `added` does not reach such a pronoun: that ruling governs an English noun answering to no morpheme at all, as `יָשְׁבוּ בָהֶּ` → *men shall dwell therein* is, and here a written nominal answers to it, so read whether the verse writes the referent before marking a supplied subject `added` or folding it into the predicate under rule 20. **But that nominal must stand earlier in the Hebrew verse than the clause whose subject the ASV supplies, and what it does where it stands is no part of the condition.** Resumption is the continuing of a referent the verse has already named, which is why the paragraphs above ask for a nominal standing earlier in the verse; so read the source order rather than the English, and read whether the nominal is there to be continued rather than what case or office it holds. A vocative, a fronted topic or any other detached noun standing before that clause is a nominal the pronoun resumes and takes the pronoun exactly as a written subject does: `אַל בָּנָי ... מַעֲבִרִים עַם־יְהוָה` → *Nay,* ***my sons*** *... **ye** make Jehovah's people to transgress* gives *ye* to `בֵּן`, headed on *sons* under this rule's closing sentence, which is also what rule 36 means in refusing to mark a vocative's supplied *ye* `added`. Where instead the verse's only mention of that referent stands after that clause and inside a clause of its own, nothing there is being continued: the supplied pronoun answers to no morpheme this clause reaches and is its own `added` unit under rule 20's closing sentence, whatever a neighbouring verse names, since rule 10 makes the verse the whole unit of work. `מֵקִים מֵעָפָר דָּל ... כִּי לַיהוָה מְצֻקֵי אֶרֶץ` → ***He*** *raiseth up the poor out of the dust ... For the pillars of the earth are Jehovah's* leaves that *He* `added`, the name being written only as the predicate possessor of a later causal clause, while `יְהוָה מֵמִית וּמְחַיֶּה מוֹרִיד שְׁאוֹל וַיָּעַל` → *Jehovah killeth, and maketh alive:* ***He*** *bringeth down to Sheol, and bringeth up* gives its *He* to the `יְהוָה` standing at the head of the verse, and 1SA.2.6 and 1SA.2.8 are the two shapes in one chapter. The cataphoric case below is the limit of this and not a counter-example: `בְּפֶה חָנֵף` writes its possessive before the lexeme-bearing word inside a clause the noun itself stands in, which is a reordering this rule allows, and not a reach forward into a clause the noun has nothing to do with. **But the morpheme those sentences look for is one the verse writes as a nominal of its own, and a finite verb's inflection is not one.** Where the only morpheme in the verse denoting that referent is the person and number of a finite verb, rule 17 has already realized it as that verb's own subject pronoun, and a further subject pronoun the ASV supplies for a coordinated verbless clause answers to nothing left in the verse: it is its own `added` unit under rule 20's closing sentence, while the copula joins the predicate as that rule directs. `יִצְפֹּן לַיְשָׁרִים תּוּשִׁיָּה מָגֵן לְהֹלְכֵי תֹם` → ***He*** *layeth up sound wisdom for the upright;* ***He*** ***is*** *a shield to them that walk in integrity* gives the first *He* to `יִצְפֹּן` under rule 17, leaves the second `added`, and puts the *is* on `מָגֵן`. Read what the verse writes rather than what the passage is about, since a referent named in a neighbouring verse is not written in this one and rule 10 makes the verse the whole unit of work; where the verse does write the nominal, the preceding paragraph governs as before. **But a morpheme already holding a pronoun of its own is not a home for a second one.** Where more than one morpheme in the verse denotes that referent, each takes only the English written for it, as rule 51 says of a waw and rule 43 of a spent preposition: the object suffix of `מְצָאנֻהוּ` above takes the *him* of *find him out* under rule 18, and the further *He* goes to `שַׁדַּי`. Count the ASV's realizations against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s. **And where the two realizations are not of the same kind, the head goes to the one writing the noun's own lexeme, whichever of them stands first.** The direction to head on the first English occurrence settles a tie between realizations of one kind — two *he*s, two *from*s, or a noun and the pronoun resuming it in that order — and it is not a preference for the phrase's left edge. Where the ASV realizes one written nominal both by a pronoun and by the word that writes its lexeme, rule 24 governs and the head is the lexeme-bearing word, exactly as rule 18 heads a twice-written suffix on the pronoun that realizes it directly rather than on the generic noun beside it, and as rule 31 keeps a head off a word the ASV supplied. This reaches a construct chain whose *nomen rectum* the ASV promotes to the clause's English subject while writing the chain's own relation as a possessive on the head noun: `בְּפֶה חָנֵף יַשְׁחִת רֵעֵהוּ` → *With* ***his*** *mouth* ***the godless man*** *destroyeth his neighbor* gives both *his* and *the godless man* to the one `חָנֵף`, headed on *godless*, while `פֶּה` keeps its own *mouth*, and `וּבְהַוַּת בֹּגְדִים יִלָּכֵדוּ` → *But* ***the treacherous*** *shall be taken in* ***their own*** *iniquity* divides the same way, headed on *treacherous*. Such a possessive is not `added` under rule 18's closing sentence and the promoted subject is not `added` under rule 17: a morpheme in the phrase answers to each, which is the count the paragraph above runs. Read which English word writes the lexeme before reaching for the first occurrence, since Hebrew writes the possessor after its head noun while English writes the possessive before it, so the pronoun stands first as often as not. **But every sentence above places a further realization of the nominal itself, and a pronoun the ASV supplies to complete an English verb's valency is not one.** Where the Hebrew writes no object morpheme on the verb and no object marker in the clause, and the English verb reaches its object only through a pronoun the ASV has written — `וַיִּשְׂאוּ וַיָּבִאוּ אֶל־דָּוִד` → *and* ***took it*** *and* ***brought it*** *to David* — rule 44's supplied-object clause governs and that pronoun is its own `added` unit, however plainly a noun standing earlier in the verse names what it denotes. Reading such a pronoun as a resumption would leave that clause nothing to govern, since a supplied object is supplied precisely because the verse has already named the thing, and rule 44's own `וַיַּפֵּל` → *he let* ***it*** *fall* and `וַיַּשְׁקְ` → *gave* ***them*** *drink* would be resumptions too. What the sentences above place is a subject the clause writes no word for, or a second realization of the nominal inside a phrase the Hebrew writes, as the *him* of `עַל־אֱלוֹהַּ` is the object of the very preposition that noun stands under. So read what the English pronoun completes and not only what it denotes: a supplied subject in a verbless clause is this rule's — `וְעֵץ חַיִּים תַּאֲוָה בָאָה` → *when the desire cometh,* ***it*** *is a tree of life* gives its *it* to `תַּאֲוָה` — and a supplied object of a written verb is rule 44's. Where an object morpheme does stand it takes the pronoun under rule 18 as before, and one verse may write both, as 2SA.23.5 does in giving the *it* of *it is all my salvation* to `בְּרִית` and leaving the *it* of *he maketh it not to grow* `added`. **But an expletive the ASV writes to fill a subject slot English cannot leave empty realizes no referent at all, whatever the verse writes.** Where the ASV extraposes a clausal subject the Hebrew writes — an infinitive phrase, or another clause the ASV renders in full further on — and puts an anticipatory *it* where that subject would stand, the pronoun denotes nothing the verse names and rule 20 governs it: it is its own `added` unit, while the predicate keeps the copula that rule gives it and the extraposed clause keeps its own English. `תוֹעֲבַת כְּסִילִים סוּר מֵרָע` → ***it*** *is an abomination to fools to depart from evil* leaves that *it* `added`, with *is an abomination* on the construct noun and *to depart* on the infinitive. What the sentences above place is a pronoun denoting a referent the verse names and the ASV has rendered by a word of its own, so read what the pronoun stands for before folding it into a written morpheme's unit: `וְעֵץ חַיִּים תַּאֲוָה בָאָה` → *when the desire cometh,* ***it*** *is a tree of life* gives its *it* to `תַּאֲוָה`, which the ASV has already written as *the desire*, and one chapter may write both shapes, as PRO.13.12 and PRO.13.19 do. **An interrogative particle or a negative whose scope covers coordinated clauses is read the same way.** Where the Hebrew writes `הֲ` or `לֹא` once in the first of two coordinated clauses and the ASV rewrites it at the head of the second, every occurrence belongs to that one morpheme's discontinuous unit, headed on the first: `הֲלוֹא מַחֲזֵה־שָׁוְא חֲזִיתֶם וּמִקְסַם כָזָב אֲמַרְתֶּם` → ***Have*** *ye* ***not*** *seen a false vision, and* ***have*** *ye* ***not*** *spoken a lying divination* gives both *have*s to the `הֲ` and both *not*s to the `לֹא`, while each verb keeps only its own subject pronoun and lexical verb. This is rule 55's reading of a subordinator the ASV rewrites over a coordinated clause, applied to the particle that governs one. The second occurrence is neither `added` under rule 30 nor folded into the second clause's verb under rule 17. **Where in that first clause the morpheme stands is no part of the condition, and neither is a repetition of the same English word.** What licenses the second occurrence is that the morpheme's scope reaches the second clause, so a negative predicating of a verbless clause governs a coordinated colon from the middle of the first as readily as from its head, and the ASV answers it with whatever word carries the negation where that colon opens — a *Nor* or a *neither* as readily as a second *not*. `שְׂאֵת פְּנֵי־רָשָׁע לֹא־טוֹב לְהַטּוֹת צַדִּיק בַּמִּשְׁפָּט` → *To respect the person of the wicked is* ***not*** *good,* ***Nor*** *to turn aside the righteous in judgment* gives both *not* and *Nor* to the one `לֹא`, headed on the first. Read the clause's scope rather than the morpheme's position, exactly as rule 51 reads a postposed *also*, and do not mark such a word `added` under rule 14's closing sentences because no conjunction stands in the second colon: what that count marks is a coordinator no morpheme answers to, and what distinguishes a *Nor* from a bare *and* is the negation the written negative is there to license, as rule 35 says in heading such a word on the negative. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. But read what is actually written before applying it: where the Hebrew gaps the morpheme in the second line and a waw stands there, and the ASV writes a single word carrying both the coordination and the negation, rule 35 governs and that word goes to the waw, as `לֹא עֲלִיתֶם ... וַתִּגְדְרוּ` → *Ye have not gone up ..., neither built up* leaves the *neither* to the waw alone; and where no conjunction morpheme stands in that colon at all, rule 35's fusion has no coordination to rest on and the distributed reading above governs.
amendments.why: This chapter analysed one construction two ways: 2SA.23.5 folded a supplied object pronoun into the noun that names its referent under this rule's resumption sentences, while 2SA.23.16 marked the identical construction `added` under rule 44, both verses writing the referent's noun earlier in the verse. The over-broad sentence is this rule's own — *every English realization of that referent belongs to the noun's one possibly discontinuous unit* — which on its face reaches a pronoun the ASV supplies to complete an English verb's valency and would leave rule 44's supplied-object clause nothing to govern, since a supplied object is supplied precisely because the verse has already named the thing; rule 44's `וַיַּפֵּל` → *he let it fall* and `וַיַּשְׁקְ` → *gave them drink* would both be resumptions. The added limit narrows this rule where it stands rather than leaving a cross-reference for whoever reads it first, and it changes nothing else: the resumption examples this rule already carries are a supplied subject and an oblique inside a phrase the Hebrew writes, both of which the new sentence names and keeps. The corpus supplied for this chapter bears on neither rule and so contradicts nothing.

conventions: A pronoun the ASV supplies for a referent the verse names is placed by what it completes, not by what it denotes. A subject pronoun filling a slot a verbless clause leaves empty joins the nominal's unit under rule 25 — 23.5 *For it is all my salvation* goes to `bərîṯ` — while a pronoun completing an English verb's valency where the Hebrew writes no object morpheme is `added` under rule 44, as 23.5 *he maketh it not to grow* and 23.16 *took it* and *brought it* are. A noun standing earlier in the verse is not evidence for the first reading, since a supplied object is supplied precisely because the verse has already named the thing.

A supplied third-person subject pronoun in a verbless clause joins a participial predicate, whose gender and number are what the pronoun answers to: 23.19 gives *he* and 23.23 *He was* to `niḵbāḏ`. It is `added` under rule 20's closing sentence where the predicate carries no agreement at all — a comparative or other prepositional phrase — and no nominal in the verse denotes the referent, which is 23.4's *He shall be as the light*, the ruler being named in 23.3 and rule 10 making the verse the whole unit of work. The competing reading marks the participial cases `added` as well, on the ground that rule 17's permission names a finite verb.

`bə` before a numeral rendered *one of* takes the whole partitive expression, the preposition being the morpheme that states the partitive relation: 23.9 `bišlōšāh` → *one of the three mighty men*, 23.24 `baššəlōšîm` → *was one of the thirty*, the copula joining the preposition there under rule 49. Rule 15's `added` partitive is not reached, since it governs a quantifier no morpheme in the clause licenses. The same preposition takes a bare *among* wherever the ASV writes one (23.18, 23.22).

Do not absorb unrelated intervening words into that unit. **Where English repeats one source function word because its scope is distributed across coordinated or emphatically repeated phrases or clauses, every English occurrence belongs to that source morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit.** `מִן` in `מִבּוֹא בְדָמִים וְהוֹשֵׁוַע` → *from bloodguiltiness, and from avenging* takes both occurrences of *from*, while the waw takes only *and*; `בִּי אֲנִי` → *upon me ... upon me* gives both occurrences of *upon* to the single preposition while the suffix and explicit pronoun take their respective *me*. The repeated English word is neither `added` nor reassigned to a neighboring source item merely to make the units contiguous. **And the repeated word need not be one the source writes.** Where another rule assigns a supplied English function word to a morpheme's unit — a preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own object under rule 44, or a word the ASV supplies for a bare nominal under rule 33 — and the ASV writes that same word again over an elliptical or gapped parallel member, the second occurrence belongs to that same morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit on exactly the terms above, however much stands between. `תְּבַקְשֶׁנָּה כַכָּסֶף וְכַמַּטְמוֹנִים תַּחְפְּשֶׂנָּה` → *search* ***for*** *her as* ***for*** *hid treasures* gives both *for*s to the verb, since the second stands for the searching the comparative clause elides, while each comparative `כְּ` takes only the *as* written for it. Do not read such a repetition as a second English word for the preposition, the conjunction or the comparative particle it stands beside, which would give one morpheme a two-word rendering the ASV writes for it nowhere else; and do not mark it `added` under rule 30, since the morpheme that licensed the first occurrence licenses this one. Read the clause's scope rather than the morpheme's position, exactly as rule 51 reads a postposed *also*, and do not mark such a word `added` under rule 14's closing sentences because no conjunction stands in the second colon: what that count marks is a coordinator no morpheme answers to, and what distinguishes a *Nor* from a bare *and* is the negation the written negative is there to license, as rule 35 says in heading such a word on the negative. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. But read what is actually written before applying it: where the Hebrew gaps the morpheme in the second line and a waw stands there, and the ASV writes a single word carrying both the coordination and the negation, rule 35 governs and that word goes to the waw, as `לֹא עֲלִיתֶם ... וַתִּגְדְרוּ` → *Ye have not gone up ..., neither built up* leaves the *neither* to the waw alone; and where no conjunction morpheme stands in that colon at all, rule 35's fusion has no coordination to rest on and the distributed reading above governs.
amended.why: This chapter analysed one construction two ways: 2SA.23.5 folded a supplied object pronoun into the noun that names its referent under this rule's resumption sentences, while 2SA.23.16 marked the identical construction `added` under rule 44, both verses writing the referent's noun earlier in the verse. The over-broad sentence is this rule's own — *every English realization of that referent belongs to the noun's one possibly discontinuous unit* — which on its face reaches a pronoun the ASV supplies to complete an English verb's valency and would leave rule 44's supplied-object clause nothing to govern, since a supplied object is supplied precisely because the verse has already named the thing; rule 44's `וַיַּפֵּל` → *he let it fall* and `וַיַּשְׁקְ` → *gave them drink* would both be resumptions. The added limit narrows this rule where it stands rather than leaving a cross-reference for whoever reads it first, and it changes nothing else: the resumption examples this rule already carries are a supplied subject and an oblique inside a phrase the Hebrew writes, both of which the new sentence names and keeps. The corpus supplied for this chapter bears on neither rule and so contradicts nothing.

report: Checked all 47 lemma groups in the candidate table, then read the dump end to end for the `added` units the table is blind to. One genuine split, and it was in that blind spot: a pronoun the ASV supplies for a referent the verse has already named. 2SA.23.5 folded both supplied *it*s into `בְּרִית` under rule 25's resumption sentences, while 2SA.23.16 marked the same construction — a supplied object pronoun with no object morpheme in the clause — `added` under rule 44 (*took it*, *brought it*), with `מַיִם` written earlier in that verse exactly as `בְּרִית` is written in 23.5.

Resolved toward 23.16, which follows rule 44's supplied-object clause as written. The competing resolution would leave that clause nothing to govern: an object is supplied precisely because the verse has already named the thing, so if resumption reached it, rule 44's own three examples would all be resumptions too. The patch touches 23.5 only — t037 (*he maketh it not to grow*) becomes its own `added` unit, while t025 (*For it is all my salvation*) stays with `בְּרִית`, that clause writing no subject word of its own and so being rule 25's proper case, the same as `וְעֵץ חַיִּים תַּאֲוָה בָאָה` → *it is a tree of life*.

Three near-misses examined and left alone as source-licensed. (1) Supplied *He* is `added` in 23.4 but joins `נִכְבָּד` in 23.19 and 23.23: a participle inflects for gender and number and the pronoun answers to that, while 23.4's predicate is a comparative phrase carrying no agreement at all and no nominal in that verse denotes the referent, rule 10 making the verse the whole unit of work. (2) `בְּ` + numeral takes *one of* whole in 23.9 and 23.24 and a bare *among* in 23.18 and 23.22 — the ASV writing two things for one relation. (3) Two-token proper names: `עֲשָׂהאֵל` fuses, `בֵּית לֶחֶם` and `אֲבִי עַלְבֹון` split, each decided by rule 30's one-English-word condition.

BSB: no genuine error among the 18 disagreements. Every one is the documented convention difference — recastings that leave a preposition nothing (23.7's `בָּ` before a promoted object, 23.16 and 23.17's `לִ` before a modal's bare complement, 23.19's two `לְ`s under rule 21), suffixes the ASV writes no pronoun for (23.8's `עֲדִינוֹ`, 23.18 and 23.22's `לוֹ` in clauses with no written subject), five articles the ASV writes no *the* for, the unrendered waw of 23.4, and the paragogic *he* of `חָלִילָה` under rule 32. Nothing here should move an accepted edge.

Three conventions recorded and one amendment returned. The amendment narrows rule 25 at the boundary it had not considered — its resumption sentences place a further realization of the nominal itself, not a pronoun supplied to complete an English verb's valency — since that boundary is what this chapter had to decide twice and settled two ways. No new rule: the participial-subject judgment and the partitive `בְּ` are recorded as conventions instead, the corpus tables supplied here bearing on neither.
